genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a trail-mapping specialist inspects the routes before the busy season
the route markers hold badly on steep rock faces

this method cuts down the number of rescue operations
she records the positions in a logbook the maintenance crews consult
text: Before the walking season opens, the mapper for a trail service goes out and checks every route she keeps. The trouble is a familiar one. Markers hold badly on steep rock faces, and hikers lose the path the moment fog rolls up the valley. She reads the slope with a clinometer, notes what the rock is made of, and picks an anchor that suits it. In hard, close-grained stone she sets a bolt sealed with resin. In crumbling, flaky rock she prefers a weighted post that frost cannot lift out. Then she stakes the route in short runs, placing each marker where a walker can still see the one behind it. That habit cuts down on rescue callouts and keeps people from turning back for no reason. Every position goes into a logbook, and the maintenance crews read it before they head out on their rounds.

units: two viewing platforms overlook the same valley

the upper platform is reached by very steep steps

the view from the lower platform is partly hidden by the cliff
the lower approach suits groups with children better
a strong wind makes the upper platform unpleasant
the writer finally judges the lower platform more satisfying
the quality of a built feature depends on the fit between a place and its public
text: Two viewing platforms open onto the same valley, and they deserve very different verdicts. The upper one sits on a rocky spur above the gorge, and reaching it is punishing work. The steps rise steeply, the rail is narrow, and the visitor arrives winded in front of a view that pays the effort back. The lower one rests on a grassy shelf, and anyone can stroll to it. What the view loses in sweep it gains in softness, since the cliff hides part of the valley. You might favor the first for its harshness, the second for the mercy it shows families with children. Yet the comparison tilts toward the lower deck as soon as the wind picks up. The high spur turns unpleasant to stand on, while the sheltered one keeps its charm. Good building owes less to height than to the fit between a site and the people it draws.

units: the writer is writing from lodging set on a slope

the drink served tastes bitter

a man minding his beasts gave them water
the writer announces a return worn out and changed
text: I am writing from an inn built into a hillside, where the wind rattles the shutters all night long. Let me hand you this trip in pieces, the way it comes back to me. The lodging first: a bare room, a hard bed, and a huge window that looks out over a dry plateau where nothing moves. The food next: warm flatbread, a goat cheese so salty it stings the tongue, and a bitter brew the keeper pours into chipped bowls. Then the walking. We set out at sunrise on tracks that wind along the slope, and we pass far more sheep and goats than we pass vehicles. One thing more, since it stayed with me. A man minding his animals stopped and handed us water without a word. Nothing here matches what I pictured before leaving. I will come home burned brown, worn out, and probably changed more than a little.

text: So what got into you, heading out alone onto that plateau? Short answer: I wanted to walk until my head had emptied itself out. Did the start go smoothly? Not even close. I missed the first bus of the day, sat under a metal shelter for half the morning, and ended up crossing the plain in whatever pickup would slow down and stop for me. And where did you sleep? Behind a dike, out of the wind, with a tarp strung between two posts. Rough night? Freezing, yes, though the sky was so clear that I gave up on sleeping and just lay there looking at it. And the way back? That is where it fell apart. A storm turned the track to running mud, and I had to backtrack the whole way to the village. Would you do it over? In a heartbeat, but with a real tent and boots that can hold their grip on loose stone.

units: the keeper of a mountain shelter describes the collapse of a path

the rescuers reached them by way of the ridge line

no casualty was reported
the footbridge is destroyed for good
local officials are considering a new route higher up
text: The keeper of a high-valley shelter tells the story of the night the trail gave way. "The rain came down without a break, and the stream doubled in size," he says. The cause is easy enough to trace, and he traces it himself. A slope stripped of its trees held nothing back, so the water ran straight off it and onto the path below. "We heard something crack, and then the whole bank slid off," he goes on. The effect was immediate. A handful of hikers found themselves stuck above the break, with no way down and nowhere else to turn. A rescue team came at them along the ridge and walked them out on a narrow, steep ledge. "Nobody was hurt, but the footbridge is gone for good," he adds. Valley officials are already studying a replacement route, higher up and clear of the channel the water carved.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: crossing a mountain range was once a risky undertaking

even experienced guides lost their bearings
the difficulty came from the lack of visible landmarks

text: Crossing a mountain range was once a gamble with poor odds. Pack trains climbed into gorges where snow wiped out the trail, and even seasoned guides lost their bearings between two slopes that looked alike. Distance was never the real problem. The problem was having nothing fixed to steer by once mist swallowed the shapes of the land. People tried piling up stones at intervals, and the wind knocked the piles flat. They tried driving in wooden poles, and the damp rotted them through. The answer came from a modest idea. Cut a notch into the rock face at shoulder height, whiten it with lime, and it stays visible under fresh snow. Drivers could then move from notch to notch without looking up at a sky that told them nothing. Every marking system we rely on now descends from that humble trick.

units: a valley shaped by ice differs from a valley shaped by a river

the side valleys of a river join the main course at the same height
text: A valley carved by ice and a valley carved by a river look different at first glance. The glacial one has a broad, flat floor and walls that rise almost straight up, because thick, heavy ice grinds the base and the sides alike. The river valley cuts a narrow, deep notch instead. Water works mainly along the line it follows, and the flanks slump in under their own weight. The mechanics explain the contrast. A glacier moves as one solid mass, slow and unrelenting, while a torrent drags pebbles that saw at the rock like a file. Side valleys tell the same story. Those feeding a former glacier arrive high above the main trough, left hanging, and spill down as waterfalls. Those feeding a river join the main channel at the same height. That one detail often settles the question in unfamiliar country.

units: the narrator reports a crossing he remembers precisely

the narrator concludes that bare ground holds many readable signs
text: I ought to set down a crossing I remember clearly, and take its aspects one at a time. The setting: a desert of stone, bare of any tree, rolling in swells that fooled the eye about distance. The march: seven stages, each begun before sunrise and closed at dusk, with a halt in the shade of a boulder through the worst of the heat. The supplies: water drawn from built cisterns that our guides found again without hesitation, hard flatbread, and a reserve of salt. The mishaps: a strap that snapped, a foot hurt on the stones, a night when the wind flattened our shelter. The encounters, last of all: a train of traders working the same track the other way, whose men warned us of a well that had been filled in. What stays with me is that dryness is not emptiness, and bare ground reads like a crowded page.

text: Pack your bag the day before you leave, never at the last minute. Start by laying your gear out flat on the floor. You will see right away what is missing and what weighs too much for what it gives you. Load the heavy things against your back, halfway up, so the weight does not pull you backward. Slide the rain layer in at the very top, where you can grab it fast. In the morning, before you leave the hamlet, fill your bottles and trace the route on the map. Find the springs and mark the steep sections. On the way, stop at regular intervals, pull off your boots, and let your feet dry out. Choose your sleeping spot while the light lasts, on dry ground, well away from streambeds. When you wake up, scatter the stones and wipe out every trace of your fire before you shoulder the bag.

units: the traffic on a plateau path rose after it spread online

the shopkeepers protest while the herders approve
text: It was supposed to be a quiet season, and it has turned into a headache for the whole valley. Ever since the plateau path started making the rounds online, the number of walkers has shot up, and the parking area overflows before sunrise. So the meadows get used as parking space, the fences give way, and the herders watch their animals wander off. Naming the cause is easy. Living with what follows is less so. The path has widened under all those boots, the plants that held the soil are gone, and rain now digs little channels down the slope. The town has decided to push back. A shuttle takes the place of cars, the number of spaces is capped, and the path closes at the start of the week to let the grass grow back. Shopkeepers grumble, herders breathe easier, and the valley waits for next season.
